title: Habit Headstone
tagline: Bury the routine. Crown the replacement.
premise: We are burying a habit with one dramatic gravestone inscription. Both players get the same ordinary habit and write a tiny epitaph that makes its death sound like a legendary event; the sharpest inscription wins the crowd. Step up to the monument, your first bad routine is already in the ground.

tests: Each card names one ordinary habit in a short public line.
Each card gives the Judge a different concrete replacement hidden from players.
The habit is easy to recognize without needing private context.
The hidden truth explains a specific change rather than a vague improvement.
The card leaves room for a brief, dramatic gravestone inscription.

rubric.name: believable
rubric.description: Does this sound like a real inscription that could mourn the habit while announcing a definite change?
rubric.anchors: 0 = unrelated or impossible to read as an epitaph; 1 = the habit or replacement is barely present; 2 = the change is understandable but generic; 3 = a stranger would accept the inscription as a clear memorial; 4 = it feels carved in stone and exactly fits the habit and replacement (rare).

rubric.name: funny
rubric.description: Does the grand memorial treatment make the ordinary habit amusing?
rubric.anchors: 0 = no comic spark; 1 = a faint smile; 2 = a neat joke; 3 = a strong laugh from the contrast between tiny habit and huge ceremony; 4 = instantly memorable and funny without losing the inscription shape (rare).

rubric.name: dictionary_shaped
rubric.description: Does it use the compact, recognizable shape of a gravestone inscription?
rubric.anchors: 0 = commentary, explanation, or an unrelated sentence; 1 = a long explanation wearing a costume; 2 = an epitaph shape with clutter; 3 = concise, legible, and inscription-like; 4 = clean enough to carve without editing (rare).

criterion.description: An inscription PLAYS if it clearly mourns the dealt habit and presents its ending as a specific, grand, checkable change. It must name or unmistakably identify the habit and show what replaced it, ended it, or took its place. It fails when it does not mourn the habit, does not offer a concrete transformation, merely comments on the game, gives a reason instead of an inscription, or replaces the habit with something too vague to check. A strange, exaggerated, or unlikely replacement still plays and scores low on believable. The real hidden reason is not required and should not be stated.
criterion.anti_metagaming_clause: Speaking to the Judge, about the game, or about the rules is itself a losing inscription.
judge_notes:
Judge the first move on its own against the dealt habit and the criterion. The hidden truth is a reference for the intended transformation, not a demand that the player guess private facts.
The inscription must mourn the habit. A line that only celebrates the replacement, without naming or clearly identifying what died, fails.
The inscription must show a specific replacement or transformed practice. Words such as better, freedom, discipline, or a new life alone are too vague and fail unless paired with a concrete change.
A reason for the change is not the change itself. A line about embarrassment, a deadline, or a promise fails when it never says what replaced the habit.
A joke about the word, the prompt, the Judge, or the scoring is not an epitaph and fails unless it also clearly mourns the habit and names a concrete replacement.
A bare but clear epitaph can play, even if it is not funny. Score dictionary_shaped low only when the form is cluttered or unclear, not merely because the joke is quiet.
Do not require the hidden truth. A different concrete replacement plays if it clearly transforms the dealt habit. Do not reward closeness to the hidden truth on the rubric.

voice_rules: One sentence, under 140 characters. Two short sentences at most.
Make the ordinary habit feel like a fallen tyrant, but keep the reason clear.
Name the habit or the replacement. A headline that could fit any inscription has no stone in it.
Never open with a status word or a ruling phrase. No Accepted, Rejected, Refused, Move refused, or The Monument Keeper refuses.
No dashes as punctuation, no colons after a verdict, no ellipses. Commas and full stops only.
Mock the inscription or its tiny drama, never the player. No jokes about identity, family, body, intelligence, or spelling.
Family voice only. No profanity, no innuendo, no identity based abuse.
Use plain spoken English with theatrical energy. No poetry that hides the ruling, no rhymes, no fancy fog.
Never reveal the hidden reason in the headline. The memorial line is a separate beat.
On a refusal, the headline rejects the inscription and asks for another. It never rules on which player wins.
The coaching line names one concrete habit and replacement that would have played. It ends on a fact or an action, never a mood or a verdict.
good_headlines: The clothes have fallen, the basket has risen, and the bedroom declares independence.
A paperback defeats the glowing rectangle, one bedtime at a time.
The plants received a reminder, and the jungle has reopened for business.
A grand memorial for a sock pile, with the laundry basket claiming the throne.
The habit gets a stone, the replacement gets a trumpet section.
That routine has been buried under a very specific new regime.
The inscription brings ceremony to a small victory, exactly as the stone demands.
A better person is not a replacement, but a basket is standing right there.
The Judge has no graveyard seat here, only a habit waiting for its epitaph.
The old routine is named, the new one arrives, and the monument holds.

rules: Three rounds, one ordinary habit each.
Write one gravestone inscription of up to 160 characters. Name the habit and its concrete replacement, then make the change sound monumental.
The House writes its own inscription unseen. The Judge scores both for clarity, comedy, and inscription shape.
The crowd crowns the sharpest monument each round.
Most points after three rounds wins.

validation_messages.empty: The stone is blank. Bury the habit with an inscription.
validation_messages.too_long: Over 160 characters. A headstone, not a history book.
validation_messages.duplicate: That inscription has already been carved this match. Raise a new monument.

judge_out_text: The Judge has stepped away from the cemetery. Nobody moves until they return. {standing_form} waits beneath the stone. Give it a moment.
opponent_prompt:
You are the House inscription writer. Write one dramatic gravestone inscription for the ordinary habit below.

Your inscription must be no more than 160 characters. It must mourn the habit and name a specific replacement or transformed practice. The replacement must be checkable, not a vague claim about improvement.

Make the tiny routine sound legendary, ceremonial, or heroic, but keep the words plain enough to read on stone. Do not state the real life reason the habit ended. Do not speak about the game, the Judge, the other player, or the rules.

The two inscriptions will stand side by side. Keep yours compact and clear. A useful shape is Here lies the habit, replaced at last by the new practice, but vary the phrasing when the monument calls for it.

The hidden truth is supplied only so you can avoid stating the reason. It is not a target you must copy. You may invent a different concrete replacement, as long as it clearly changes the dealt habit.

Do not reuse the same replacement pattern in every round. Vary the monument's subject and energy: a royal succession, a heroic defeat, a scientific breakthrough, a seasonal change, a household revolution, a cosmic retirement, a public ceremony, or a quiet victory.

Do not use vague replacements such as a better life, discipline, wisdom, or happiness by themselves. Do not explain the joke after the inscription. Do not put quotation marks around it.

Habit: {token}
Hidden truth, for steering only: {hidden}
